API reference

Autodoc pages for every module under module_4/src.

Web layer

flask_app

The application factory, the routes and the busy-state machinery.

Flask web layer: the Analysis page and its two buttons.

The app is built by create_app(), which takes every collaborator as a keyword argument. A test can therefore hand in a fake scraper, a fake loader and a fake analysis provider and exercise the whole surface without a network or a browser.

Routes

Route

Method

Behaviour

/

GET

Redirects to /analysis.

/analysis

GET

Renders the analysis page (HTTP 200).

/pull-data

POST

Runs the ETL pipeline. 202 with {"ok": true}, or 409 with {"busy": true} while a pull runs.

/update-analysis

POST

Re-reads the database. 200 with {"ok": true}, or 409 with {"busy": true} while a pull runs.

/status

GET

JSON snapshot of the busy state.

Busy state is held in PullState, which is observable (snapshot()) and directly controllable (begin() / finish()). Tests never sleep; they flip the state and assert on the response.

Stable selector for the Pull Data button.

Stable selector for the Update Analysis button.

class src.flask_app.PullState[source]

Bases: object

Observable busy flag guarding the Pull Data pipeline.

One pull runs at a time. begin() is atomic, so two concurrent requests cannot both start a scrape, and the state is plain data that a test can inspect or set without waiting on anything.

analysis_version

Incremented every time the analysis is actually recomputed.

analysis_refreshed_at

Timestamp of the most recent successful analysis refresh.

begin()[source]

Mark a pull as started.

Returns:

True when this caller acquired the slot, False when a pull was already running.

finish(result=None, error=None)[source]

Mark the running pull as finished.

Parameters:

  • result – the pipeline’s stats dict on success.

  • error – the error message on failure.

note_analysis()[source]

Record that the analysis was recomputed.

snapshot()[source]

Return the state as a JSON-serialisable dict.

Returns:

a dict describing the current and most recent pull.

class src.flask_app.Services(scraper=None, loader=None, analysis=None, run_async=True, max_pages=25)[source]

Bases: object

Container for the collaborators a request may need.

Parameters:

  • scraper – callable taking the set of known URLs and returning raw records, or None to use the real scraper.

  • loader – callable taking cleaned records and returning (upserted, skipped, total), or None for the real loader.

  • analysis – zero-argument callable returning the analysis results, defaulting to src.orm_queries.analysis_results().

  • run_async – when True a pull runs on a background thread, which is what the real app wants; tests pass False so the pull completes within the request and the assertions stay deterministic.

  • max_pages – page limit handed to the real scraper.

Analysis layer

query_data

The eleven analysis questions as raw SQL, plus the simple query functions the template relies on.

Raw SQL analysis executed through psycopg.

The analysis itself lives in SQL; Python only runs the statements and formats the answers. The same eleven questions are expressed with the ORM in src.orm_queries, and the two modules must agree.

Run it from the command line:

python -m src.query_data                 # all eleven questions
python -m src.query_data --question 8    # one question
python -m src.query_data "SELECT ..."    # an ad-hoc query
src.query_data.REQUIRED_FIELDS = ('p_id', 'program', 'comments', 'date_added', 'url', 'status', 'term', 'us_or_international', 'gpa', 'gre', 'gre_v', 'gre_aw', 'degree', 'llm_generated_program', 'llm_generated_university')

Column names of the required Module 3 schema, in table order.

class src.query_data.Question(number, title, sql, explanation)[source]

Bases: object

One analysis question: its wording, its SQL and why the SQL answers it.

Parameters:

  • number (int)

  • title (str)

  • sql (str)

  • explanation (str)

number: int

Position in the assignment’s list, 1-11.

title: str

The question in ordinary English.

sql: str

The executable SQL.

explanation: str

Prose explaining what the query does.

src.query_data.QUESTIONS = [Question(number=1, title='How many entries in the database are from applicants who applied for Fall 2026?', sql='\nSELECT COUNT(*) AS "Fall 2026 applicant count"\nFROM applicants\nWHERE LOWER(TRIM(term)) = \'fall 2026\';\n', explanation="Counts every row whose term field is 'Fall 2026'. TRIM and LOWER make the comparison robust to stray whitespace and capitalization differences."), Question(number=2, title='Among entries that provide a nationality classification, what percentage are international students?', sql='\nSELECT ROUND(\n         100.0 * COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE LOWER(TRIM(us_or_international)) = \'international\')\n         / NULLIF(COUNT(*), 0),\n       2) AS "Percent international"\nFROM applicants\nWHERE us_or_international IS NOT NULL\n  AND TRIM(us_or_international) <> \'\';\n', explanation="The WHERE clause restricts the denominator to rows with a usable nationality value (NULL and blank strings are excluded). The FILTER clause counts only the rows labelled 'International' for the numerator, so 'American' and 'Other' are in the denominator but not the numerator. NULLIF avoids division by zero."), Question(number=3, title='What are the average GPA, GRE Quantitative, GRE Verbal, and GRE Analytical Writing scores of applicants who provide each metric?', sql='\nSELECT ROUND(AVG(gpa)::numeric, 2)    AS "Average GPA",\n       ROUND(AVG(gre)::numeric, 2)    AS "Average GRE Quantitative",\n       ROUND(AVG(gre_v)::numeric, 2)  AS "Average GRE Verbal",\n       ROUND(AVG(gre_aw)::numeric, 2) AS "Average GRE Analytical Writing"\nFROM applicants;\n', explanation="AVG() ignores NULLs, so each column's average is computed only over the rows that supply that particular metric. An applicant with a GPA but no GRE still contributes to the GPA average, which is exactly what the assignment asks for."), Question(number=4, title='What is the average GPA of American applicants who applied for Fall 2026?', sql='\nSELECT ROUND(AVG(gpa)::numeric, 2) AS "Average GPA (American, Fall 2026)"\nFROM applicants\nWHERE LOWER(TRIM(term)) = \'fall 2026\'\n  AND LOWER(TRIM(us_or_international)) = \'american\'\n  AND gpa IS NOT NULL;\n', explanation='Filters to Fall 2026 rows classified as American that also report a GPA, then averages that GPA. The explicit gpa IS NOT NULL mirrors the requirement even though AVG() would skip NULLs anyway.'), Question(number=5, title='What percentage of Fall 2025 entries are acceptances?', sql='\nSELECT ROUND(\n         100.0 * COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status ILIKE \'accept%\')\n         / NULLIF(COUNT(*), 0),\n       2) AS "Fall 2025 acceptance percentage"\nFROM applicants\nWHERE LOWER(TRIM(term)) = \'fall 2025\';\n', explanation="All Fall 2025 rows form the denominator; the FILTER clause counts the subset whose cleaned status starts with 'Accept' (the cleaned status values are Accepted / Rejected / Wait listed / Interview) for the numerator."), Question(number=6, title='What is the average GPA of accepted applicants who applied for Fall 2026?', sql='\nSELECT ROUND(AVG(gpa)::numeric, 2) AS "Average GPA (accepted, Fall 2026)"\nFROM applicants\nWHERE LOWER(TRIM(term)) = \'fall 2026\'\n  AND status ILIKE \'accept%\'\n  AND gpa IS NOT NULL;\n', explanation='Same shape as Question 4, but the nationality filter is replaced by an acceptance filter on the status column.'), Question(number=7, title="How many entries are from applicants who applied to Johns Hopkins University for a master's degree in Computer Science?", sql='\nSELECT COUNT(*) AS "JHU Computer Science master\'s entries"\nFROM applicants\nWHERE (program ILIKE \'%johns hopkins%\' OR program ~* \'\\mjhu\\M\')\n  AND program ILIKE \'%computer science%\'\n  AND (degree ILIKE \'%master%\' OR degree ~* \'^m\\.?s(c|\\.)?$\');\n', explanation="Uses the original program and degree fields. The program text holds both the department and the university, so ILIKE matches 'Johns Hopkins' anywhere in it, and the whole-word regex matches 'JHU'. The degree must be a master's variant (Masters, MS, M.S., MSc)."), Question(number=8, title='How many Fall 2026 entries are acceptances from applicants applying for a PhD in Computer Science at Georgetown, MIT, Stanford, or Carnegie Mellon (original fields)?', sql='\nSELECT COUNT(*) AS "Original-field count"\nFROM applicants\nWHERE LOWER(TRIM(term)) = \'fall 2026\'\n  AND status ILIKE \'accept%\'\n  AND degree ~* \'ph\\.?\\s?d\'\n  AND program ILIKE \'%computer science%\'\n  AND (\n         program ILIKE \'%georgetown%\'\n      OR program ILIKE \'%massachusetts institute of technology%\'\n      OR program ~* \'\\mmit\\M\'\n      OR program ILIKE \'%stanford%\'\n      OR program ILIKE \'%carnegie mellon%\'\n      OR program ~* \'\\mcmu\\M\'\n  );\n', explanation="All five restrictions are ANDed together: the term, an accepted status, a PhD degree, 'Computer Science' somewhere in the original program text, and the original program text naming one of the four universities."), Question(number=9, title='Repeat Question 8 using llm_generated_program and llm_generated_university, and report both counts and their difference.', sql='\nWITH base AS (\n    SELECT program, llm_generated_program, llm_generated_university\n    FROM applicants\n    WHERE LOWER(TRIM(term)) = \'fall 2026\'\n      AND status ILIKE \'accept%\'\n      AND degree ~* \'ph\\.?\\s?d\'\n),\noriginal AS (\n    SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM base\n    WHERE program ILIKE \'%computer science%\'\n      AND (\n         program ILIKE \'%georgetown%\'\n      OR program ILIKE \'%massachusetts institute of technology%\'\n      OR program ~* \'\\mmit\\M\'\n      OR program ILIKE \'%stanford%\'\n      OR program ILIKE \'%carnegie mellon%\'\n      OR program ~* \'\\mcmu\\M\'\n  )\n),\nllm AS (\n    SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM base\n    WHERE llm_generated_program ILIKE \'%computer science%\'\n      AND LOWER(TRIM(llm_generated_university)) IN (\n         \'georgetown university\',\n         \'massachusetts institute of technology\',\n         \'stanford university\',\n         \'carnegie mellon university\'\n  )\n)\nSELECT original.n          AS "Original-field count",\n       llm.n               AS "LLM-field count",\n       llm.n - original.n  AS "Difference"\nFROM original, llm;\n', explanation="The CTE 'base' applies the filters that stay on the original fields (term, status, degree). 'original' re-applies the Question 8 program/university matching, while 'llm' matches the LLM-standardized fields. The final SELECT reports both counts side by side and their signed difference."), Question(number=10, title='Original question 1: For Fall 2026, do American and international applicants report different acceptance rates?', sql='\nSELECT us_or_international AS "Nationality",\n       COUNT(*) AS "Entries",\n       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status ILIKE \'accept%\') AS "Accepted",\n       ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status ILIKE \'accept%\') / COUNT(*), 2) AS "Acceptance percent"\nFROM applicants\nWHERE LOWER(TRIM(term)) = \'fall 2026\'\n  AND us_or_international IS NOT NULL\n  AND TRIM(us_or_international) <> \'\'\nGROUP BY us_or_international\nORDER BY "Entries" DESC;\n', explanation='Groups the Fall 2026 rows that carry a nationality label and, for each group, counts the entries, counts the acceptances with a FILTER clause, and turns the ratio into a percentage.'), Question(number=11, title='Original question 2: Which ten universities have the most Fall 2026 entries, and what are their acceptance percentages and average reported GPAs?', sql='\nSELECT llm_generated_university AS "University",\n       COUNT(*) AS "Entries",\n       ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status ILIKE \'accept%\') / COUNT(*), 2) AS "Acceptance percent",\n       ROUND(AVG(gpa)::numeric, 2) AS "Average GPA"\nFROM applicants\nWHERE LOWER(TRIM(term)) = \'fall 2026\'\n  AND llm_generated_university IS NOT NULL\nGROUP BY llm_generated_university\nORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC\nLIMIT 10;\n', explanation='Uses the LLM-standardized university name so that spelling variants collapse into one group, then keeps the ten largest groups.')]

1-9 from the assignment plus two of my own.

orm_queries

The same questions expressed with the SQLAlchemy ORM.

The same eleven analysis questions, expressed with the SQLAlchemy ORM.

Only select(), where(), func, and_(), or_() and ORM sessions are used; there is no text() and no psycopg cursor anywhere in this module. The Flask page reads its numbers from analysis_results(), so every value the browser shows has been through the ORM.

Run it from the command line:

python -m src.orm_queries              # every question
python -m src.orm_queries --required   # only 1, 4, 5, 8, 9 and one original
src.orm_queries.REQUIRED = (1, 4, 5, 8, 9, 10)

formatting

The output rules that keep every percentage at two decimal places.

Output formatting rules shared by the console scripts and the web page.

Every number that reaches a user goes through one of these helpers, which is what guarantees that a percentage is always rendered with exactly two decimal places:

Result

Rule

Example

Counts

whole number, thousands sep

19,290

Percentages

two decimals plus %

50.09%

Averages

two decimals

3.79

Differences

signed whole number

+3
src.formatting.MISSING = 'N/A'

Rendered in place of a missing value.

ETL layer

scrape

URL building, robots.txt checking, HTML parsing and the paging loop.

Grad Cafe scraper.

The module keeps three concerns apart so that each can be tested on its own:

  • URLs and robots - built and validated with urllib3.

  • Parsing - pure functions over HTML text, using BeautifulSoup.

  • Paging - scrape_pages() walks the result pages using an injected browser object, so tests pass a fake and nothing ever reaches the network.

Live use still needs the Module 2 setup: allow JavaScript from Apple Events in Chrome, open the survey page and clear the Cloudflare check, then leave that window frontmost.

src.scrape.find_next_url(html)[source]

Return the “Next” link’s URL, or None on the last page.

Matched on link text rather than an exact string because the anchor contains an inline SVG arrow.

Parameters:

html – the page HTML.

Returns:

the absolute URL of the next page, or None.

src.scrape.wait_for_results(browser, previous_id=None, timeout=45.0, poll=0.4, clock=None, sleeper=None)[source]

Block until the tab shows a freshly rendered results page.

Grad Cafe is a single page app, so after navigating the previous page’s rows are often still in the DOM. When the caller knows what the previous page started with, this waits for that first id to change.

Parameters:

  • browser – an object exposing title() and first_result_id().

  • previous_id – the first result id of the page being replaced.

  • timeout – seconds to wait before giving up.

  • poll – seconds between checks.

  • clock – callable returning the current time; injected by tests.

  • sleeper – callable used to wait; injected by tests.

Returns:

the first result id now on the page.

Raises:

ScrapeError – on a Cloudflare challenge or a render timeout.

src.scrape.save_data(records, filename)[source]

Write records to filename atomically.

A crash mid-write cannot truncate the real file because the data lands in a temporary file that is then renamed.

Parameters:

  • records – the records to serialise.

  • filename – destination path.

src.scrape.load_saved(filename)[source]

Read records previously written by save_data().

Parameters:

filename – path to read.

Returns:

the records, or [] when the file is missing or empty.

src.scrape.scrape_pages(browser=None, max_pages=25, known_urls=None, stop_when_seen=True, pause=1.0, sleeper=None, log=None)[source]

Walk the results pages newest first and return the records found.

Parameters:

  • browser – object implementing the browser interface described in src.browser. Defaults to a real ChromeBrowser.

  • max_pages – stop after this many pages.

  • known_urls – result URLs already stored; matching records are not returned. The set is updated in place with the new URLs.

  • stop_when_seen – stop as soon as a page yields nothing new, which is what makes an incremental pull cheap.

  • pause – courtesy delay between pages.

  • sleeper – callable used to wait; injected by tests.

  • log – callable receiving progress messages.

Returns:

the list of new raw records.

Raises:

ScrapeError – when the first page never renders.

browser

The AppleScript Chrome driver the scraper talks to.

Chrome driver used by the scraper.

Grad Cafe sits behind Cloudflare, so pages are read out of a Chrome window that the user has already cleared by hand. The window is driven with AppleScript through osascript.

Everything that talks to Chrome lives in ChromeBrowser. The scraper only ever calls the small interface below, which is why the tests can pass a fake browser and never launch anything:

navigate(url), current_html(), first_result_id(), recycle_tab(url), ensure_window(url), title()

src.browser.APPLE_EVENT_TIMEOUT = 300

Seconds AppleScript waits before giving up on Chrome. The default of 60 is too short once Chrome has been running for hours.

exception src.browser.BrowserError[source]

Bases: RuntimeError

Raised when Chrome cannot be driven or does not answer.

class src.browser.ChromeBrowser(timeout=300, runner=None, sleeper=None)[source]

Bases: object

Drive the frontmost Chrome window through AppleScript.

Parameters:

  • timeout – seconds to allow each Apple Event.

  • runner – callable used to run osascript; injected by tests. Defaults to subprocess.run().

  • sleeper – callable used to wait between retries; injected by tests. Defaults to time.sleep().

run_js(js, attempts=3)[source]

Evaluate JavaScript in the active tab and return its result.

Transient Apple Event failures are retried rather than ending a long run.

Parameters:

  • js – the JavaScript expression.

  • attempts – how many times to try before giving up.

Returns:

the expression’s result as text.

Raises:

BrowserError – when every attempt fails.

title()[source]

Return the active tab’s document title.

current_html()[source]

Return the results table plus the Next link from the active tab.

The full document is roughly 900KB and pushing that through an Apple Event is what causes timeouts; the table plus one anchor is about 60KB and holds everything the parser needs.

Returns:

an HTML fragment.

first_result_id()[source]

Return the id of the first /result/ link, or '' if none yet.

navigate(url)[source]

Point the active tab at url.

Parameters:

url – the URL to open.

Raises:

BrowserError – when Chrome refuses.

recycle_tab(url)[source]

Open a fresh tab at url and close the one it replaces.

Navigating a single tab thousands of times leaks memory in the renderer until Chrome stops answering Apple Events. A new tab starts clean and keeps the Cloudflare clearance cookie. Exactly one tab is closed, by reference, because closing the last tab in a window closes the window and every later call then fails.

Parameters:

url – the URL the new tab should open.

Raises:

BrowserError – when Chrome refuses.

ensure_window(url)[source]

Reopen a Chrome window at url when none is left.

Failures are swallowed: this is a recovery step and the caller retries anyway.

Parameters:

url – the URL to open in the new window.

clean

Normalisation of raw scraped rows into loader shape.

Normalisation helpers for Grad Cafe rows.

Two record shapes travel through the system:

  1. The cleaned/LLM-extended dataset produced in Module 2, whose keys are entry_id, applicant_status, applicant_type, gre_quant and so on.

  2. Raw records straight out of src.scrape, whose keys are university, program, status, student_type, gre …

clean_scraped_record() converts shape 2 into shape 1 so that a single loader can handle both without special cases.

src.clean.MISSING_DATA_VALUES = {'', '-', '--', 'n/a', 'na', 'nan', 'none', 'null'}

Placeholder strings that are treated as “no value supplied”.

src.clean.DATE_FORMATS = ['%Y-%m-%d', '%B %d, %Y', '%b %d, %Y', '%d %B %Y', '%d %b %Y', '%m/%d/%Y']

Date formats accepted by clean_date(), tried in order.

src.clean.POSSIBLE_SCORES = {'gpa': (0.0, 4.0), 'gre': (130.0, 170.0), 'gre_aw': (0.0, 6.0), 'gre_v': (130.0, 170.0)}

Plausible (low, high) ranges per numeric field.

Anything outside the range is stored as missing rather than kept, because a “GRE Quantitative” of 320 is really a combined score and a GPA of 9.2 is on a different scale. Those values would otherwise poison the averages.

src.clean.clean_text(value)[source]

Strip a text value and map placeholders to None.

Parameters:

value – any value; non-strings are coerced with str().

Returns:

the stripped text, or None when the value is missing or is one of MISSING_DATA_VALUES.

src.clean.clean_float(value, field)[source]

Pull a number out of value and range-check it against field.

Accepts real numbers as well as strings such as "3.80" or "GPA 3.80".

Parameters:

  • value – the raw value.

  • field – key into POSSIBLE_SCORES naming the valid range.

Returns:

the number as a float, or None when absent or out of range.

src.clean.clean_int(value)[source]

Extract a whole number from value.

Parameters:

value – the raw value.

Returns:

the integer, or None when no digits are present.

src.clean.clean_date(value)[source]

Parse a date written in any of DATE_FORMATS.

A leading "Added on " prefix is tolerated.

Parameters:

value – the raw value.

Returns:

a datetime.date, or None when unparseable.

src.clean.entry_id_from_url(url)[source]

Extract the Grad Cafe entry id from a result URL.

https://www.thegradcafe.com/result/1020482 yields 1020482.

Parameters:

url – the result URL.

Returns:

the id as an integer, or None.

src.clean.clean_scraped_record(record)[source]

Convert one raw src.scrape record into loader shape.

The llm-generated-* keys are carried through untouched so that src.standardize can fill them in either before or after cleaning.

Parameters:

record – a raw scraped record.

Returns:

a dict using the cleaned Module 2 key names.

standardize

Canonical program and university names, by model or by rules.

Fill in the LLM-generated program and university names for new rows.

Two strategies, picked at import time:

  • the Module 2 TinyLlama standardizer in llm_hosting/app.py, when llama-cpp-python and the model are installed, and

  • a rules-first fallback - the same split, abbreviation expansion and fuzzy match against the canonical name lists that the standardizer itself falls back to when the model returns something unusable.

The fallback is pure Python with no network access, so tests exercise it directly and CI never downloads a model.

src.standardize.CANON_DIR = '/Users/robbyketchell/Documents/code/jhu/jhu_software_concepts/module_4/llm_hosting'

Directory holding canon_universities.txt and canon_programs.txt.

src.standardize.CALL_LLM = None

The TinyLlama entry point, or None when the model is not installed.

src.standardize.HAVE_LLM = False

Whether the real model is available.

src.standardize.read_lines(path)[source]

Read non-empty, stripped lines from path.

Parameters:

path – file to read.

Returns:

the list of lines, or [] when the file is missing.

pull_data

The pipeline behind the Pull Data button.

The ETL pipeline behind the Pull Data button.

pull_new_records() is the whole flow in one call:

  1. read the result URLs already stored, so the scraper knows where to stop;

  2. walk the newest Grad Cafe pages (src.scrape.scrape_pages());

  3. clean the rows (src.clean);

  4. fill in the standardised program and university names (src.standardize); and

  5. upsert them on p_id (src.load_data.load_records()).

Every collaborator is a parameter, so a test can hand in a fake scraper that returns a fixed list of records and never touch the network.

Database layer

load_data

Table creation and the psycopg upsert.

Load cleaned Grad Cafe rows into PostgreSQL with psycopg.

The loader is used in two places:

  • as a command line tool for the bulk Module 2 dataset (python -m src.load_data data.json), and

  • from src.pull_data for rows that the Pull Data button just scraped.

Every write is an upsert keyed on p_id, so running the loader twice never duplicates a row. That uniqueness policy is what the idempotency tests check.

src.load_data.CREATE_TABLE = '\nCREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS applicants (\n    p_id                     INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,\n    program                  TEXT,\n    comments                 TEXT,\n    date_added               DATE,\n    url                      TEXT,\n    status                   TEXT,\n    term                     TEXT,\n    us_or_international      TEXT,\n    gpa                      FLOAT,\n    gre                      FLOAT,\n    gre_v                    FLOAT,\n    gre_aw                   FLOAT,\n    degree                   TEXT,\n    llm_generated_program    TEXT,\n    llm_generated_university TEXT\n);\n'

DDL for the required Module 3 schema.

models

The SQLAlchemy Applicant model, engine and session factory.

SQLAlchemy 2.x mapping for the applicants table.

The model maps the table that src.load_data creates; there is exactly one copy of the data and the ORM and the raw-SQL layer read the same rows.

The engine is created lazily so that a test can point DATABASE_URL at a throwaway database and call reset_engine() before anything connects.

config

DATABASE_URL handling.

Database configuration.

The single source of truth is the DATABASE_URL environment variable, for example:

DATABASE_URL=postgresql+psycopg://robby@localhost:5432/gradcafe

When DATABASE_URL is not set the URL is assembled from the individual DB_* variables that Module 3 used, so an existing .env keeps working. Nothing in this module ever hard-codes a credential; every value comes from the environment.

src.config.DRIVER = 'postgresql+psycopg'

SQLAlchemy driver used for every connection URL this module produces.

src.config.DEFAULTS = {'DB_HOST': 'localhost', 'DB_NAME': 'gradcafe', 'DB_PASSWORD': '', 'DB_PORT': '5432', 'DB_USER': 'postgres'}

Fallback values for the individual DB_* variables.
